q: French Protestant refugees were granted farms in a mountain-ringed valley east of Cape Town from 1688, and the valley still carries a name meaning French corner. Which valley?
exp: The Huguenots brought vine-growing experience the Dutch settlers lacked, and their surnames are still on estates there three centuries later. The valley is closed on three sides, which keeps the floor warm and still while the slopes above it stay cooler.

q: One Cape governor founded a town on the Eerste River in 1679 and planted a farm of his own on the slopes behind Cape Town six years later. Who was he?
exp: Stellenbosch is named for him, and so is Simonsberg. The farm he took for himself behind Table Mountain, Constantia, became the source of the sweet wine that made the Cape famous in Europe, so one governor stands behind both the country's leading red district and its most famous sweet wine.

q: Formed in 1918 and given statutory power a few years later, a growers' co-operative fixed minimum prices and handed out production quotas until the system was dismantled in the 1990s. Which body was that?
exp: It was formed to cope with a grape surplus, and for seventy years it rewarded volume over quality: a quota was worth more than a good site, and high-cropping varieties were planted where they had no business being. Deregulation, and the end of the export boycott, are why so much of the modern Cape vineyard has been replanted.

q: A label names a single pocket of ground inside a district rather than the district itself, telling the buyer the fruit came off that one patch. Which Wine of Origin tier is that tighter name?
exp: The scheme nests geographical unit, region, district and ward, with the ward as the tightest tier and the one defined on soil, climate and ecology rather than on administrative convenience. A ward is where a Cape label gets closest to naming a piece of ground.

q: Vintage and variety claims on a Cape label each need eighty-five percent of the wine behind them. The origin claim is stricter than that. What does it demand?
opts: Every grape must come from the named area
The same eighty-five percent as the other two claims
Ninety percent of the grapes from the named area
Ninety-five percent of the grapes from the named area
exp: Origin is absolute in this system, which is worth knowing because the other two claims are not. A wine labelled Stellenbosch Cabernet Sauvignon 2019 was grown entirely in Stellenbosch, but may legitimately hold fifteen percent of another grape and fifteen percent of another year.

q: A visitor buys a bottle at a cellar door and the label reads Wine of Origin Estate. What has that phrase committed the producer to?
opts: The whole property lies inside a single ward
The grapes were grown and the wine made on the registered unit
The wine was bottled on site but the fruit may have been bought in
The property has been in one family for at least three generations
exp: An estate is registered as a production unit, so the claim is about farming and vinification happening in the same place. It says nothing whatever about quality, and a great many of the Cape's best wines are made from bought-in fruit and cannot use the term at all.

q: Registering a block as a single vineyard in South Africa carries a restriction no other origin tier imposes. What is capped?
opts: The size of the block, at six hectares
The finished alcohol, at fourteen percent
The yield, at fifty hectolitres per hectare
The planting density, at ten thousand per hectare
exp: The block must also be planted to one variety, so the designation means a genuinely single parcel rather than a marketing name. Six hectares is small enough that the wine really can be the expression of one site, which is the whole point of registering it.

q: One Wine of Origin region exists solely for fortified wine and overlays Paarl, Tulbagh and Wellington. Which region?
exp: Boberg is the oddity in the scheme: a region that sits on top of districts already covered by the Coastal Region, and that may be used only for fortified styles. The Klein Karoo makes a great deal of fortified wine but is an ordinary region covering every style.

q: Certification of a Cape wine's origin, vintage and variety claims is handled by a statutory body rather than by the producers themselves. Which body?
exp: The board runs the scheme and issues the seal, which is why a Cape origin claim is auditable rather than merely asserted. SAWIS is a real organisation doing a different job, gathering the industry's statistics, and the Cape Winemakers Guild is a voluntary association of winemakers.

q: Since 2010 the sticker sealing a certified Cape bottle has carried a second guarantee alongside origin, vintage and variety, traceable through the number printed on it. What else does it certify?
opts: That no sulphur dioxide was added at any stage
That vineyard and cellar were run sustainably
That the vineyard was never irrigated
That residual sugar stays below a stated level
exp: The Integrated Production of Wine scheme audits farming and cellar practice against the industry's sustainability standards, and folding it into the same seal made participation close to universal. The number can be entered on a public site to trace the bottle back, which is unusual transparency for a national scheme.

q: Weathered granite lies beneath the mountain foot slopes of Stellenbosch, Paarl and the Paardeberg, and growers farming without irrigation prize it. What does it give them?
opts: Enough fertility to push yields well past what quality allows
Drainage so free that daily irrigation becomes unavoidable
A strongly alkaline soil that has to be corrected before planting
A clay-rich soil that holds winter rain through a dry summer
exp: Granite breaks down to a deep reddish soil with real clay content, and that clay is a reservoir deep enough for the vine to draw on through months without rain and still finish the season. It is a large part of why unirrigated bush vines are possible on these slopes in a climate where the growing season is essentially dry.

q: The pale, quartz-rich rock that forms the cliffs above Cape Town also underlies vineyard soils across the winelands, and it is acidic and desperately poor in nutrients. What is it called?
exp: It weathers to a bleached, sandy, low-vigour soil that usually needs lime before it will grow anything, and it drains hard. Wines off it tend to be lean and taut rather than broad, which is exactly why growers chasing a finer style go looking for it.

q: Swartland growers talk constantly about the shale beneath their bush vines, a rock laid down long before anything with a shell existed. Which shale?
exp: Malmesbury shale is Precambrian, and it splits into plates roots can follow down through. It alternates with granite intrusions such as the Paardeberg across the district, and growers there will name which of the two a wine came off as readily as a Burgundian names a slope.

q: Rock beneath the Cape vineyards runs to hundreds of millions of years old, and in places far older than that, which is ancient even by the standards of the wine world. What has that age done to the soils above it?
opts: It has made them unusually rich in organic matter
It has made them uniformly alkaline
It has left them too shallow for roots to pass a metre
It has stripped them of their nutrients
exp: Soils formed on young volcanic or glacial material are still releasing minerals; soils weathered for this long have had theirs leached away. Low natural vigour suits quality, but it also means the Cape grower is managing an impoverished soil rather than restraining a fertile one.

q: Granite foot slopes below the mountains, Cabernet-led reds, the country's main viticulture faculty and its oldest wine route all belong to a single district. Which one?
exp: The district runs from sandy flats near the water up to slopes well above three hundred metres, so one name covers a wide range of sites and styles. The wine route opened in 1971 and was the first in the country, which is much of why the town became the industry's centre of gravity.

q: Stellenbosch reaches south toward a large bay, and the afternoon wind coming off it is why the district ripens later than its inland neighbours. Which bay?
exp: The south-easter crosses that water before it reaches the vineyards, and the blocks closest to it pick latest. Table Bay lies on the other side of the peninsula at Cape Town, Saldanha is well up the west coast, and Walker Bay is a hundred kilometres east at Hermanus.
